overview: Americans vote in the midterm elections today, with control of Congress at stake. Markets head into the vote with tech shares under pressure and oil prices swinging on whether the US and Iran can reach a deal to end their war. In New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani threatened legal action against federal immigration authorities over reported use of city lots as staging areas. Abroad, the Spain train collision death toll and a reported $6.3 billion Binance hack are drawing wide attention.

stories.headline: Supreme Court rejects Trump administration bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots
stories.summary: The Supreme Court declined a Trump administration request to order California election officials to set aside mail ballots from about 20,000 people the administration says are noncitizens. The ruling came the day before the midterms. Separately, Bloomberg reports an appeals court lifted a lower-court order that had limited federal demands on election officials.
stories.why_it_matters: The ruling means the disputed California ballots are expected to be counted in the normal way. It also shows how courts are handling last-minute federal efforts to intervene in how states run elections.
stories.background: The Justice Department has pressed states over voter eligibility ahead of the 2026 midterms. On Monday the administration asked the Supreme Court on an emergency basis to act on California mail ballots it alleges came from noncitizens. Lower courts had ruled against some of the administration's demands on election officials. The Supreme Court's refusal, according to the BBC, essentially ends the administration's bid to disqualify the ballots in California.

facts.text: The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Monday to order California election officials to set aside mail ballots from 20,000 people it alleges are noncitizens.
The Supreme Court rejected the request.
The BBC reported the ruling essentially ends the administration's bid to disqualify the ballots in California.
CNBC reported the request came as the Justice Department appeals the dismissal of a lawsuit over Alaska's Senate election.

Bloomberg reported that a US appeals court halted a judge's order that barred the administration from demanding officials set aside certain ballots or threatening criminal prosecutions around the midterms.
The Hindu reported that another federal judge found the administration's last-minute demands of California election officials violated the Constitution.

stories.headline: Election Day arrives with control of Congress at stake after record early voting
stories.summary: Americans vote Tuesday in midterm elections that will decide control of the House and Senate. Early voting was high in several states, and outlets say final results could take days. Strategists quoted by the New York Times see Democrats as likely to retake the House, with the Senate more uncertain.
stories.why_it_matters: The outcome will shape whether the president faces a Congress controlled by the opposition party for the next two years, affecting budgets, investigations and legislation. Results may not be clear on election night, so early leads can mislead.
stories.background: Every House seat and about a third of Senate seats are on the ballot. Polls cited by outlets show voters focused on affordability. The president is not on the ballot, but the contests are widely seen as a verdict on his term. Outlets list Texas, Maine, Iowa, Kansas and Michigan among the notable Senate races. Results begin arriving at 6 p.m. ET from Kentucky and Indiana.

facts.text: Results start coming in at 6 p.m. ET from Kentucky and Indiana, NPR reported.
Strategists in both parties say Democrats are likely to win back the House, while the Senate battle is more complicated, the New York Times reported.
France 24 reported more than 58 million ballots were cast in record early voting.
The Center Square reported 40% of registered voters in Texas cast ballots early, a record, and early turnout in Georgia set a midterm record.
About 690,526 people voted early in New York City, according to Board of Elections data cited by the Brooklyn Paper.
Axios reported that the first votes counted Tuesday will probably look redder than the final result, and control of Congress could take days to settle.
AP reported the election comes after a year in which President Trump has tried to interfere in how states run elections and cast doubt on the outcome.
AP reported the Texas Senate race between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico is unusually competitive.

stories.headline: Rep. Haley Stevens endorses Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race, angering Democrats
stories.summary: Michigan Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed in the Senate race on the eve of the midterms. Many Democrats condemned the move and House leaders were reported to be weighing action. Stevens defended it in a social media post.
stories.why_it_matters: Michigan's Senate seat is among the races that could decide control of the Senate, so a late crossover endorsement draws national attention.
stories.background: Michigan's open Senate race pits Rogers, a former Republican congressman, against El-Sayed, a Democrat who won his party's nomination. Stevens had earlier been a Democratic Senate contender, and Gov. Gretchen Whitmer endorsed her in July, according to the Washington Examiner. Stevens and El-Sayed had a falling-out during the campaign. On Sunday she withdrew her support for him and backed Rogers.

The endorsement came on the day Stevens was scheduled to appear with El-Sayed in a show of party unity, NewsNation reported.

Fox News reported House Democratic leaders are considering action against Stevens.
Vice President JD Vance said the endorsement would give some Michigan voters permission to back Rogers, Fox News reported.
The Washington Post reported the El-Sayed campaign had a $2.4 million fundraising day as Stevens endorsed his opponent.

stories.headline: Judge dismisses case against two ex-FBI officials accused of lying about Hunter Biden probe
stories.summary: Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui dismissed charges against former FBI officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, who were accused of lying to Congress about the Hunter Biden investigation. Outlets report the judge said the case lacked probable cause and was rushed ahead of the midterms.
stories.why_it_matters: The ruling is a setback for Justice Department prosecutions of figures the president has criticized. It also feeds the debate over whether prosecutions are being timed for political effect.
stories.background: Floris and Benavides were FBI officials involved in the investigation of Hunter Biden, the former president's son. The Justice Department charged them with falsely suggesting to Congress that they were unaware of federal investigations around Hunter Biden. Faruqui is a federal magistrate judge in Washington. The department can still choose how to respond to the dismissal.

The two were accused of falsely suggesting to Congress that they were not aware of federal investigations around Hunter Biden, CBS reported.
Reuters and CNBC reported the judge indicated the charges were rushed ahead of the midterm election.
AP reported the judge cited 'weaponization' in tossing the charges.

stories.headline: New York reports first measles death in more than 30 years
stories.summary: New York health officials said a child in Lewis County died in connection with the state's measles outbreak, the first measles death in the state in over 30 years. The state has reported 178 cases this year, and Gov. Kathy Hochul tied the death to falling vaccination rates.
stories.why_it_matters: Measles spreads easily among unvaccinated people, and falling vaccination rates raise the risk of outbreaks and deaths. Parents should check that children's measles shots are current.
stories.background: The US declared measles eliminated in 2000 after maintaining high vaccination rates. Coverage has since dropped below the 95% level needed to prevent outbreaks, The Hindu reported. About four weeks ago Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency over the outbreak. Lewis County is in northern New York, roughly 400 miles from New York City.

New York has reported 178 measles cases this year.
Hochul said the death reflected eroding vaccination levels.

stories.headline: Nine killed in Learjet crash in Florida neighborhood; investigators focus on weather
stories.summary: A Learjet 60 on a flight from Austin to the Bahamas crashed into a residential area in Palm Beach County, Florida, killing nine people. Victims include two young children and a 20-year-old co-pilot. The NTSB expects weather to be a major focus.
stories.why_it_matters: The NTSB investigation may produce findings about icing and flight safety. For most people this is a regional tragedy.

stories.headline: US strikes Iran's Qeshm Island, calls it defensive, as deal talk continues
stories.summary: The US carried out limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz late Monday, and a US official described them as defensive. Reports say the targets were surface-to-air missile launchers and radar equipment. The strikes came hours after Vice President JD Vance said he was optimistic about diplomacy to end the eight-month-old war, and an Iranian official said the two sides remain far from a deal.
stories.why_it_matters: The war and the Hormuz shipping lane affect oil prices and so fuel and shipping costs. Oil rose after the strikes, a sign of how sensitive markets are to the talks.
stories.background: The US and Iran have been in open conflict for about eight months. The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway through which a large share of the world's oil passes, and Qeshm is the largest island in it. Washington and Tehran have recently signalled openness to a diplomatic solution, but fighting and talks have continued side by side. The strikes came the night before US midterm elections.

stories.headline: Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site kills at least 29; US-mediated talks set for Nov. 10-11
stories.summary: A Russian aerial attack on an aid distribution centre and nearby shelter in a village in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region killed at least 29 people, with 48 still missing, according to reports on Tuesday. It followed an overnight barrage across the country that also hit power plants. Separately, US envoy Steve Witkoff announced US-mediated Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, which the Kremlin confirmed.
stories.why_it_matters: The strike shows the toll on civilians seeking basic aid, and attacks on power plants raise the prospect of outages as winter nears. The Abu Dhabi talks are the next test of whether the war can move toward a settlement.
stories.background: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine is in its fifth year. A rare, short humanitarian truce had just ended in neighbouring Kherson before the strike. Diplomatic efforts led by the US were suspended in February because of the war in Iran, and are now set to restart. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was also due to visit Berlin on Tuesday for talks with Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

facts.text: A Russian strike on an aid site in Ukraine's south killed at least 29 people, with 48 still missing, as of Tuesday.
Zelensky said Russia launched 289 attack drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles across nine regions overnight.
Kyiv officials said at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village; Zelensky called the attack 'utterly horrific'.
The attack came hours after a rare ceasefire ended.
Witkoff said the US will mediate Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11.
The Kremlin confirmed the talks.

stories.headline: North Korea denies US claim it stole more than $6 billion from Binance
stories.summary: North Korea rejected US allegations that its hackers stole about $6 billion from the Binance crypto exchange, with Kim Jong Un's sister Kim Yo Jong calling the FBI claim a provocation. Binance said outflows had normalised after customers withdrew about $4.6 billion, and its co-CEO said the company is financially strong. Researchers say the stolen funds were split up and are expected to take months to launder.
stories.why_it_matters: Binance holds funds for millions of users worldwide, and a theft of this size tests trust in crypto exchanges. If the US attribution holds, it would also show how much cyber theft funds North Korea's government.
stories.background: Binance is one of the world's largest cryptocurrency exchanges. Earlier this week the exchange was hit by a hack described as the largest in crypto history, and the FBI said North Korean hackers were responsible. North Korea has been linked to earlier large crypto thefts, which it has also denied. Blockchain tracing firms are following the stolen tokens across networks.

facts.text: North Korea denied involvement, calling the US allegation 'absurd rhetoric' in state media, per Reuters.

stories.headline: US to remove South Africa and Rwanda from AGOA duty-free trade program
stories.summary: The Trump administration said it will cut South Africa and Rwanda from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), saying both are breaking the program's rules. South Africa will lose its duty-free benefits from next year. The move comes about a week after the US Treasury sanctioned Rwanda's defence ministry.
stories.why_it_matters: AGOA gives duty-free US access to more than 1,800 products, so exporters and workers in both countries face higher costs and possible job losses. US importers of affected goods may also see prices change.
stories.background: AGOA is a US program that gives eligible sub-Saharan African countries duty-free access to the US market for many products. It has been a centerpiece of US economic engagement with the region. Relations between Washington and Pretoria have been strained, and the US has recently sanctioned Rwanda's defence ministry. South Africa's government said it had responded constructively to US concerns before the decision.

facts.text: The Trump administration said South Africa and Rwanda are breaking the rules of AGOA.
South Africa will be removed from the program's duty-free benefits from next year.
South Africa's government had 'constructively responded' to US concerns beforehand, per Daily Maverick.
The pact gives duty-free access for more than 1,800 products.

stories.headline: Supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe hit by second suspected cyberattack
stories.summary: Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries, including Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg and Estonia, reported refrigerator and freezer temperatures rising overnight, spoiling food. It is the second such incident in about three weeks after a similar attack in France. Europe and the US military are investigating, and the culprit has not been identified in the coverage.
stories.why_it_matters: Internet-connected equipment in shops can be tampered with to cause physical damage and food waste, which can raise costs for stores and shoppers. Axios noted that US supermarkets use similar technology.
stories.background: Modern store refrigeration is often connected to the internet so operators can monitor and control it. Last month a defrosting attack hit shops in France. This week's incident spread across multiple countries, prompting questions about who is behind it and why. The incident also highlights how vulnerable supply chains are to cyberattacks.

facts.text: Chains in at least seven countries reported cooling unit temperatures rising overnight.
The incident follows a similar attack in France about three weeks earlier.
The New York Times reported that Europe and the US military are investigating.
Temperatures in some stores reportedly soared past 100 degrees, per CBS News.

stories.headline: Cyclone Murasu makes landfall in India's Andhra Pradesh, second cyclone in a week
stories.summary: Cyclone Murasu crossed the coast near Ongole in Andhra Pradesh on Tuesday morning, bringing heavy rain to eastern India. It is the second cyclone to hit the area in a week and prompted evacuations of thousands of people. India's weather department said it had weakened into a cyclonic storm and was expected to fade into a deep depression by midnight.
stories.why_it_matters: Heavy rain and storm damage can disrupt travel, homes and power for people along the coast. Train services in the state were cancelled or diverted.
stories.background: The Bay of Bengal coast of India is regularly struck by cyclones in the October-November season. Authorities evacuate coastal residents before landfall. Murasu follows another cyclone that hit the same region days earlier. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) issues the warnings.

facts.text: Cyclone Murasu crossed the coast near Ongole in Andhra Pradesh between 3:30 a.m. and 8:30 a.m. on Tuesday.
It is the second cyclone to hit the area in a week, and thousands of people were evacuated.
The IMD said the storm weakened into a cyclonic storm, with a deep depression expected by midnight.
Trains in Andhra Pradesh were cancelled, diverted or rescheduled.

stories.background: Armed gangs control large parts of Haiti, including much of the capital. An international force has been deployed to help Haitian police push back. The gang leader's letter asks the UN to mediate rather than fight. The digest's summaries do not say how the UN or the Haitian government responded.

stories.headline: Apple beats revenue forecasts in new CEO's first report, but shares fall on margin outlook
stories.summary: Apple reported record September-quarter sales in its first earnings report under CEO John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September. Revenue came in above analyst expectations, but the stock fell about 4.5% in premarket trading Tuesday, according to MarketWatch, on a softer gross-margin outlook and slower growth in services revenue. Palantir also fell about 8% after its own results, CNBC reported.
stories.why_it_matters: Apple is one of the largest holdings in most index funds and retirement accounts, so a drop in its shares moves ordinary savers' balances. A weaker margin outlook can also hint at pricing pressure on devices.
stories.background: Apple is the world's most valuable consumer-technology company, best known for the iPhone, Mac and its services business such as the App Store and iCloud. Tim Cook ran the company for about 15 years before handing the job to John Ternus, a longtime hardware executive, in September. Investors had high expectations for Ternus's first full report. Gross margin, the share of revenue left after the cost of making products, is closely watched because tariffs and component costs can squeeze it.

Apple's results beat analyst revenue expectations, per the AP and the New York Post.

Palantir shares dropped about 8% after its earnings, CNBC reported.
The Wall Street Journal's market live blog said stock futures were mixed after Apple's earnings disappointed.

stories.headline: Oil swings on US-Iran talks; gold and the dollar follow
stories.summary: Oil fell sharply Monday on hopes of a US-Iran deal to end their war, with US crude dropping below $100, then rebounded Tuesday on renewed doubts that an agreement is close. Higher oil fed inflation and interest-rate worries, pushing gold lower and the dollar and Treasury yields higher, according to Reuters and the Wall Street Journal. The Dow gained about 500 points Monday while the Nasdaq slid, the New York Post reported.
stories.why_it_matters: Oil prices feed directly into gasoline and shipping costs, and with inflation already elevated, they shape whether interest rates stay high for mortgages and loans.
stories.background: The US and Iran have been at war, which has disrupted oil supply from the Middle East and kept crude prices high this year. Markets now trade heavily on any sign of diplomacy. Oil is a key input to inflation, and inflation expectations drive how much the Federal Reserve and other central banks might raise or hold interest rates. Gold and the dollar often move in opposite directions to expectations about rates.

facts.text: US oil fell below $100 a barrel Monday on hopes for a US-Iran peace deal, the Daily Caller reported.
The Dow rose about 500 points Monday while the Nasdaq fell, as oil tumbled on peace-deal hopes, the New York Post reported.
The Financial Times reported oil extended its decline after Iran's president said the supreme leader had given officials certain authority over talks.
Bloomberg reported oil rose Tuesday on renewed doubts that the US and Iran are close to an agreement, and gold fell.
Reuters said gold fell as higher oil stoked inflation fears ahead of the US midterm elections.
The Wall Street Journal reported gold slid as higher oil fueled expectations of higher interest rates, and the dollar rose along with Treasury yields.

stories.headline: Anthropic reports $17 billion quarterly revenue and a $23 billion loss in amended IPO filing
stories.summary: In an updated SEC filing published Monday, Anthropic reported about $17 billion in third-quarter revenue and a net loss of about $23 billion. The revised S-1 adds financials beyond the first half of the year, which the original filing covered, and lists purchase commitments of $895.4 billion, according to CNBC. Reuters reported the company plans an Australian share offer as part of the IPO, citing CommSec.
stories.why_it_matters: A listing of one of the largest AI companies would give ordinary investors, including those in index funds, a chance to own a piece of it. The filing shows how much money AI firms are spending relative to what they earn.
stories.background: Anthropic is the AI company behind the Claude chatbot, led by CEO Dario Amodei. It unveiled its S-1, the registration document a company files with the SEC before going public, last week. That first version only included financials through the first half of the year. The new filing adds the third quarter, and the New York Times says revenue is 12 times the same quarter a year ago.

The revised S-1 lists purchase commitments of $895.4 billion, CNBC reported.

stories.headline: Markets and prices on edge as midterm elections begin
stories.summary: Stock futures were mixed Tuesday as investors weighed the midterm elections, which could change control of Congress, according to the Wall Street Journal. CNBC reported Wall Street is looking at how the results could affect stocks, Treasury yields, energy prices, banks, defense and healthcare. The Financial Times and Washington Post reported that gasoline prices are set to be the highest for an Election Day on record.
stories.why_it_matters: Gasoline and everyday costs are central issues for voters, and election outcomes can shape tax, spending and regulatory policy that affects markets and household budgets.
stories.background: US midterm elections are held halfway through a president's term and decide control of Congress. Markets pay attention because a change in control can alter budget, tax and regulatory plans. Prices for fuel have risen this year amid the Iran war, and affordability has become a top campaign theme. CNBC noted that, historically, the S&P 500 has tended to do well in the year after midterms.

stories.headline: Marvell agrees to buy Lumentum in $115 billion all-stock deal; shares of both fall
stories.summary: Marvell said it reached an all-stock agreement to buy Lumentum for about $115 billion, creating what the companies called a leader in AI connectivity. Shares of both companies fell Monday, and MarketWatch quoted shareholders criticizing the offer. CNBC reported the deal is expected to close in the first half of 2028.
stories.why_it_matters: The deal shows how much money is flowing into the chips and optical gear that link AI data centers, and investor pushback is a sign of how closely the market is judging AI spending.
stories.background: Marvell designs semiconductors for data centers and networking, and Lumentum makes optical components that move data using light. Demand for both has risen with the build-out of AI computing. In an all-stock deal, Lumentum shareholders receive Marvell shares rather than cash. Large mergers like this typically need regulatory approval, which is part of why closing is expected years away.

facts.text: Marvell agreed to buy Lumentum in a roughly $115 billion deal, Fox Business reported.

stories.headline: New Yorkers vote on Election Day after a surge in early voting
stories.summary: New York City voters go to the polls Tuesday in a governor's race between Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul and Republican Bruce Blakeman. More than 690,000 people voted early in the city, according to amNY and THE CITY. Attorney general and comptroller are also on the statewide ballot, along with two House seats Democrats hope to flip, according to the Times.
stories.why_it_matters: The results will decide who runs the state, which controls much of the city's funding, transit and housing policy. Coverage here comes from outlets on the left and center; no right-leaning outlet in the digest covered the turnout numbers.
stories.background: Hochul is seeking a full term as governor and is running against Blakeman, a Republican. Mayor Zohran Mamdani campaigned alongside Hochul and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in Queens on Sunday, the last day of early voting. Early voting opened Oct. 24. THE CITY reports affordability was one of the defining issues of the campaign.

facts.text: amNY reported 690,526 New Yorkers voted early in the city, nearly 60% more than in the last governor's race four years ago.
THE CITY reported more than 690,000 city voters cast ballots since early voting opened Oct. 24, up from more than 432,000 in 2022.
Gothamist reported early voting was lower than in 2025, the mayoral election year, but rose in majority-Black districts.
City & State reported Hochul visited Democratic neighborhoods in the city on Sunday while Blakeman went upstate.

markets.summary: US stocks were lower in the latest readings: the S&P 500 fell 1.82% in its last reported session (Oct. 30) and the Nasdaq slipped 1.07% on Monday, while the Dow rose 0.41% as oil fell on hopes of a US-Iran deal. Apple shares fell about 4.5% in premarket trading after its earnings report, with investors citing a weak gross-margin outlook, according to MarketWatch. Oil rebounded early Tuesday on doubts that a deal is close, and WSJ reported that higher oil raised expectations of higher interest rates. The 10-year Treasury yield (the rate the government pays to borrow for ten years, which influences mortgage rates) was 4.94% in the latest data, and the 30-year mortgage rate was 7.24%. Note that some figures here are a few days old because of reporting lags.

concept.explanation: A safe-haven asset is something investors buy when they fear losses elsewhere, such as gold, US Treasury bonds or sometimes the dollar. Demand rises with war, election or recession worries and falls when those ease, but gold can also drop when higher interest rates make non-interest-paying assets less attractive, as happened this week. For your wallet, safe-haven buying can push mortgage-linked Treasury yields down, while a stronger dollar makes imported goods and foreign travel cheaper.

quotes.blurb: 500 of the largest US companies. The standard scoreboard for the US stock market.

quotes.name: Nasdaq Composite
quotes.blurb: Heavy on tech companies, so it swings harder than the S&P 500 on tech news.

quotes.name: Dow Jones Industrial Average
quotes.blurb: 30 big, established US companies. The oldest and most quoted index, but narrow.

quotes.name: Fed funds rate
quotes.blurb: The overnight rate the Federal Reserve targets. Every other US interest rate keys off it.

quotes.name: 2-year Treasury yield
quotes.blurb: What the US government pays to borrow for 2 years. Moves with expectations for Fed rate changes.

quotes.name: 10-year Treasury yield
quotes.blurb: The government's 10-year borrowing cost. Mortgage rates and company borrowing costs follow it.

quotes.name: 30-year mortgage rate
quotes.blurb: Freddie Mac's weekly average for a 30-year fixed mortgage.

quotes.name: Inflation (CPI, year over year)
quotes.blurb: How much consumer prices rose over the past year. The Fed aims for about 2%.

quotes.name: Unemployment rate
quotes.blurb: Share of people looking for work who can't find it. From the monthly jobs report.

quotes.name: Crude oil (WTI)
quotes.blurb: US oil price per barrel. Feeds into gas prices and inflation.

quotes.name: Crude oil (Brent)
quotes.blurb: The global oil benchmark. Jumps on Middle East and Russia supply news.

quotes.name: Natural gas (Henry Hub)
quotes.blurb: US natural gas price at the Henry Hub in Louisiana, per million BTU. Drives heating and electricity bills.

quotes.name: US dollar index (broad)
quotes.blurb: The Fed's index of the dollar against the currencies of US trading partners. Up means a stronger dollar.

quotes.name: Euro (USD per EUR)
quotes.blurb: Dollars per euro. Up means the euro strengthened against the dollar.

quotes.name: Japanese yen (JPY per USD)
quotes.blurb: Yen per dollar. Up means a weaker yen.

quotes.name: Chinese yuan (CNY per USD)
quotes.blurb: Yuan per dollar. Beijing manages it closely, so moves are a policy signal.

quotes.name: Bitcoin
quotes.blurb: The largest cryptocurrency. Trades around the clock and swings far more than stocks.
